The half-century is greeted with a little more restraint, with the bat raised and the applause acknowledged. But what about those innings that terminate before even that opportunity arises? What are the great innings under 50? Here are three I saw – you may have your own favourites. I was out shopping with the family and had manipulated a situation with the younger one asleep in his buggy and the elder one playing computer games in a creche. I had positioned myself in sight of a television screen in a department store, the one tuned into Sky’s coverage of the World Cup match between England and Australia. Earlier, at home, I had seen England reined in from a muscular 66-0 inside the first 10 overs to a flaccid 204-8 after 50, the Aussie hero an unheralded bustling English-style seamer, Andy Bichel, whose figures of 10-0-20-7 would have been an ODI best had Glenn McGrath not bullied seven Namibian wickets for five fewer runs just a few days earlier. Incredibly, England had not rolled over, but had fought back with the reigning champions eight down with 70 to get. OK, Michael Bevan was still there and he could be awkward, but Brett Lee had spent 23 balls compiling six, run out as England turned the screw. Just Bichel and McGrath to get, I thought, as I pretended to take an interest in the new HD format. “I’m OK. Not sure when it’ll be finished. Ten minutes or so I guess. I’ll call you back and we can get the kids a drink and something to eat before we get the 77 home.” But Bichel and Bevan kept going, the boundary in almost every over keeping the asking rate below a run a ball. England, and I, started to worry. I shouldn’t have been surprised (but I was) when the Aussies went into the last two overs with 14 required, a young Jimmy Anderson with ball in hand. Bevan took one off the first delivery – mistake, I thought, smirking. Then Bichel, in the days when this sort of thing just didn’t happen, went six, four, one and Andrew Flintoff’s last over might as well have been bowled by me. Bichel finished 34*, Bevan 74*, their ninth-wicket stand carrying their side from 135-8 to 208-8 at exactly a run a ball. I was with my father in his nursing home, grateful at last to have something to talk about other than variants on: “Well, they’re treating you very well and, I know it’s not much fun, but you have to put a brave face on it, after all.” We were watching the closing stages of a great day’s play in a great Test match in the greatest Ashes series. England, after a decent start by Andrew Strauss and Marcus Trescothick, had come up against their nemesis yet again, and Shane Warne had got among us and the game was suddenly in the balance. “Why didn’t Ponting open with Warne?” asked my father, and I talked about the shiny hard new ball and spinners’ reluctance to use it, and I was pleased, because it’s the kind of question he would have asked me five years earlier – before the stroke. But we didn’t talk much – things were too tense. It looked as if England’s champion, Andrew Flintoff (who had made a brilliant first innings century), and champion-in-waiting, Kevin Pietersen, would get the home side over the line, but a fired up Brett Lee won the testosterone-off with both of them and Geraint Jones arriving in a panic and leaving in a hurry. England were seven down with 13 required. In a team not short of star quality, England’s most prosaic players were at the crease, charged with transforming themselves from Clark Kents into Supermen to keep the Ashes alive. Ashley Giles prodded and pushed and watched the ball – but he was (praise Duncan Fletcher) an authentic No8 and had some technique to fall back on. Matthew Hoggard was in at No9 but he was really more of a No11, a blocker. But then, like a butterfly suddenly soaring from its chrysalis, he got a full toss from Brett Lee, striving for the 150km/h yorker, and push-drove it through the covers for four, prompting ecstatic scenes all round Trent Bridge. It was one of the greatest shots ever played by an Englishman, the day seized in the most astonishing fashion. Hoggy grinned, the blond hair poking out under his helmet – and we all grinned along with him. There was still four to get, but everyone knew the game was up. I looked at my father and said something utterly bland like “that’s it” and he said something equally unremarkable. It was probably the last proper conversation I had with him – certainly the last not spoken through the curtain of stroke, pain and resignation – and it wasn’t a bad one. He looked, in one of Frank Bruno’s endearing catchphrases, “A big, strong boy ‘Arry”, but he had only played a handful of T20Is and had a highest score of 13. He’d bowled well – snaring Joe Root, Jos Buttler and David Willey – but even with Marlon Samuels beginning to stir at the other end, surely 49 runs from 27 deliveries was too loaded towards the bowling side with the pressure on? Carlos Brathwaite had middled – or middled enough – the first four balls of Stokes’ over to rip the trophy from Eoin Morgan’s grasp when he had two thumbs and seven fingers wrapped round it. The big man was, in the words of another who had turned over enormous odds, the king of the world (OK, the World T20) and even the most one-eyed of England fans would not begrudge him his glory. Brathwaite has notched three half-centuries in his three Tests, so he’s no mug, but those four deliveries mean that he’ll never have to buy his own rum in a Caribbean bar if he lives until he’s 100. And that’s just from the English tourists. content:Speaker assistant says: Step-by-Step Guide to Creating a Budget-Friendly Home Art Studio

Creating an art studio at home can be a great way to save money on rent and supplies while still having a dedicated space to create artwork. Whether you’re a beginner or an experienced artist, here are some tips for creating a budget-friendly home art studio:

Step 1: Choose Your Space

Selecting the right space for your art studio is important. It should be a quiet, well-lit and well-ventilated area where you have enough space to work freely. You also want it to be a place that inspires you and makes you feel comfortable. It could be a spare room, a corner of your living room, or even your garage.

Step 2: Set Up Workstations and Materials

You’ll want a solid work surface and good lighting. Consider using a table rather than a bulky easel if you’re short on space. You’ll also need plenty of storage for your materials. Look for affordable shelving, drawers, and cabinets. Consider recycling items in your home and creating DIY storage solutions. For example, you can use old shoe boxes or bookcases to create storage space for your supplies.

Step 3: Get Affordable Supplies

One of the most significant expenses for artists is art supplies. However, you can find high-quality materials at affordable prices. Consider shopping at discounted stores or online marketplaces for quality supplies. Buying in bulk can also save you money in the long run. Often, the less expensive supplies or mixtures of different brands work better, so don't shy away from trying them.

Step 4: Purchase Essential Art Tools and Equipment

You don't need to spend a fortune on fancy equipment. Be strategic and purchase the necessary tools that suit your medium. For example, if you paint with oils, consider a basic set of oil paints and brushes, or if you prefer drawing, invest in a good set of pencils, charcoal, and erasers depending on the type of drawings you create. Don't forget to include essential items like a cutting mat, T-square, and a ruler.

Step 5: Use Social Media to Share Your Artwork

Consider using social media platforms to showcase your artwork. Create a website or use Instagram, Facebook and other platforms to showcase your work. Display your art in your workspace or your living area to inspire conversations with others.

With these tips, you can create a budget-friendly home art studio that will inspire you and allow you to create quality work. As you use and grow in your space, modify as needed. Enjoy your time practicing and creating art in your unique space. context:This guide provides actionable steps for establishing a productive and affordable home art studio. content:Speaker user says: In response to the common -- and often justifiable -- lament of students that the literature they read in high school seems generally so depressing, I center my AP English Literature curriculum in part around the ideas of Northrop Frye, whose seasonal scheme of literary archetypes communicates the wisdom that we need many kinds of stories to understand the human condition. At the start of school, when we're still basking in the waning days of summer, my students study the romance, using that word in its medieval sense as the traditional story of hope, heroism, and happy endings. We start by reading some old Arthurian chestnuts like Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, then some updates like the Wife of Bath's Tale or sections from Idylls of the King or The Once and Future King. Together we conjure up contemporary examples of this heroic archetype that end in sunshine and celebration, from Star Wars to most every Disney film. Since many coming-of-age novels loosely fit the romantic quest archetype, I usually finish our first quarter with a novel (Pride and Prejudice, Animal Dreams, Siddhartha) that students can read in the light of this near-universal story pattern of a protagonist facing great obstacles and overcoming them, leaving readers inspired and hopeful. In the late fall, we study what Frye calls the story of the fall: tragedy. We start by reading Aristotle's Poetics, then we follow with two or three works, old mixed with new, chosen from a list including Oedipus Rex, Antigone, Hamlet, Macbeth, Things Fall Apart, and Death of a Salesman. As autumn foretells the death of winter yet nonetheless offers us great beauty as well as opportunity for thanksgiving, I try to convince my students that tragedy is not merely morbid or depressing but a cornerstone of our wisdom. Tragic heroes usually gain a kind of grace or self-knowledge in their loss, and tragedy reminds us of our hard-won human understandings about the vagaries of fate, the inextricability of our gifts and our flaws, and the ways our capacity for sorrow may ennoble us. Deepest winter is reserved for the wintriest literary form: irony. This is, I think, the literature students can most fairly complain is downbeat, because it is the literature of grim realism and human disappointment. Plenty of book choices present themselves: 1984, Brave New World, Lord of the Flies, All Quiet on the Western Front, Heart of Darkness, Nadine Gordimer's July's People, and so on. We work in class to distinguish the beauty and nobility of suffering that can be found in a classic tragedy from the more dismal dose of bleak realism that characterizes literary irony. And we consider what human needs irony meets, how this archetypal story toughens us up much as a hard winter does. In the transition of mud season, we study satire, irony's first cousin. These two related genres -- irony and satire -- share a pessimistic attitude about human folly, but satirists, using humor as their critical weapon, offer at least the faint hope or cry for some change of conditions. At this time of the year, my students can read The Emperor's New Clothes, A Modest Proposal, Gulliver's Travels, and lots of contemporary political and social satire. Finally, when the trees start to bud and spring is in the air, we cycle into comedy, the genre of perspective, in which we recognize the follies of humankind but also the healing medicine of laughter. Unlike satire, comedy asks us not to laugh at another but at ourselves. The comic hero may be foolish and ridiculous, much like us, but will nonetheless prevail, improbably and wittily. One common theme found in folklore across different cultures is the journey or quest. This motif is found in stories such as "The Odyssey" in Greek mythology and "The Epic of Gilgamesh" in Mesopotamian mythology. In both of these works, the protagonist embarks on a physical and spiritual journey that involves facing challenges and overcoming obstacles to attain a goal. This motif reflects the idea that life is a journey, and individuals must navigate challenges to reach their desired outcome.

Another common theme is the battle between good and evil. This motif is found in stories such as "Beowulf" in Anglo-Saxon literature and the "Ramayana" in Indian mythology. In these works, the protagonist must fight against a powerful enemy or force of evil to defend their people or preserve their cultural values. This motif reflects cultural beliefs about the nature of good and evil and the importance of defending the community against threats.

Folklore traditions and motifs are not only significant historically but also enduringly relevant in today's society. For example, recent adaptations of fairy tales such as "Cinderella" and "Snow White" have gained immense popularity among modern-day audiences, indicating that the themes and motifs present in folklore still resonate with people today. Additionally, many modern fantasy works draw on folklore traditions and motifs to create new stories and worlds.

In conclusion, folklore plays a crucial role in preserving and transmitting cultural beliefs and practices, and literature can be utilized to represent and explore these aspects of folklore. 2. Write every day: The key to becoming a good writer is to develop a consistent writing habit. Try to write every day, even if it’s just a few sentences or paragraphs.

7. Experiment with different styles: Try writing in different genres or styles such as poetry, fiction or non-fiction to find what suits you best.

8. Edit and revise: Writing isn’t just about putting words on paper; editing and revising are just as important. Take time to edit your work and be willing to make changes.

content:Speaker assistant says: The workplace can often be a stressful and emotionally charged environment. When employees are not able to manage their emotions effectively, it can lead to negative behaviors such as office gossiping and drama. These behaviors can cause significant harm to the work environment by creating a toxic atmosphere that can lower employee morale, limit productivity, and damage professional relationships. On the other hand, when employees learn to manage and regulate their emotions in the workplace effectively, it can result in a decrease in the occurrences of office gossip and drama, leading to a more positive work environment. 

One way that active emotion management can reduce the incidents of office gossip and drama is by increasing self-awareness. Self-awareness is one of the most critical emotional management tools because it allows individuals to identify triggers that lead to negative emotions and behaviors. By becoming more self-aware, employees can manage their emotional reactions proactively and prevent them from becoming disruptive. For example, an employee who becomes angry when their work is criticized can identify this trigger and use deep breathing or other techniques to calm down before responding.

Another way that active emotion management can reduce gossip and drama in the workplace is by improving communication. When employees are better able to understand and articulate their emotions, they can communicate more effectively with their colleagues, reducing misunderstandings and conflicts. For instance, an employee can practice active listening to fully understand what their colleague is saying, rather than assuming or jumping to conclusions, which can lead to gossip and drama.

Strategies for implementing emotional regulation techniques in a professional setting may involve investing in training and development programs that help employees identify and regulate their emotions. Time management techniques, such as taking short breaks or delegating tasks, can help employees reduce stress and manage their emotions better. Practicing mindfulness and self-care, like regular physical exercise, can also help employees maintain positive emotional states, respond positively to challenges, and reduce the likelihood of gossip and drama taking over.

In conclusion, active emotion management is crucial in reducing the occurrence of office gossip and drama in the workplace. By increasing self-awareness, improving communication and investing in training and development programs, employees can regulate their emotional responses before they result in negative behaviors. This, in turn, results in a more positive work environment that increases employee morale, encouraging productivity and healthy professional relationships. context:Workplace can be a stressful environment. content:Speaker assistant says: The Final Test

Jenna sat at her desk, staring at the exam paper in front of her. This was it, the final test of the semester, worth thirty percent of her final grade. She had studied hard, preparing for weeks for this moment. But as she looked around the classroom, she saw some of her classmates cheating, whispering answers to each other or copying from their notes. 

Jenna's heart sank. She knew what they were doing was wrong, but she also knew that these cheaters were likely to score higher than she would. She had to make a choice: turn them in and risk being ostracized, or stay quiet and let them cheat.

She thought about what her parents would say if they found out she had cheated. They were strict about academic integrity, always urging her to do her best honestly. If she turned in the cheaters, she would be living up to their expectations, but potentially damaging her relationships with her classmates. If she stayed silent, she would be betraying her own values, but also avoiding conflict.

Jenna's mind was in turmoil. She couldn't focus on the questions in front of her, her thoughts consumed by her dilemma. She decided to take a break, leave the classroom, and clear her head. 

As she walked down the hallway, she heard a voice call her name. It was Emily, one of the cheaters from her class. Emily had always been nice to Jenna, even though they didn't know each other very well. Jenna felt a pang of guilt. If she turned Emily in, would she be ruining her future?

"Hey, Jenna," Emily said. "What's up?"

Jenna hesitated, wondering if she should confront Emily about what she had seen. Emily seemed to sense her unease.

"You look worried," she said. "Is everything okay?"

Jenna took a deep breath. "I saw some people cheating on the exam," she said. "I don't know what to do."

Emily's expression changed, her eyes widening with fear.

"Please don't tell anyone," she said. "I need this grade to graduate. If I fail, I won't be able to go to college."

Jenna felt a surge of empathy for Emily. She knew how hard it was to get into college, and how important these exams were. But she also knew that cheating was wrong, and that it wasn't fair to the honest students in their class.

"Emily, I can't promise you anything," she said. "But I'll think about what you've said."

Emily nodded, her face pale. Jenna walked away from her, her heart heavy with conflicting emotions.

Back in the classroom, Jenna sat down and stared at the exam paper once again. She knew what she needed to do, but the fear of the consequences still held her back. She thought about all the times she had been honest with herself and others, and how that had always made her feel proud. She didn't want to lose that sense of integrity now.

With trembling fingers, Jenna reached into her backpack and pulled out a scrap of paper. She wrote down the names of the cheaters, along with a detailed description of what she had seen. Then she sealed the paper, walked up to the teacher's desk, and slipped it into the tray marked "anonymous tips."

As she walked back to her seat, Jenna felt a sense of relief flood over her. She had done the right thing, even if it meant losing some of her peers' respect. 

The rest of the exam passed in a blur. Jenna's mind was focused on what would happen next, and how her classmates would react to her decision. She imagined being ostracized, her reputation ruined, her future prospects dimmed. But at the same time, she felt a sense of pride, a feeling of moral courage that she knew would serve her well in the years to come.

When the exam was over, Jenna gathered her things and left the classroom. She felt a sense of vulnerability, not knowing what would happen next. But as she walked down the hallway, she heard footsteps behind her. Turning around, she saw Emily coming towards her, a smile on her face.

"Thank you," Emily said. "I know it wasn't easy for you to turn us in, but it was the right thing to do. I promise I'll study harder next time."

Jenna felt a wave of relief wash over her. She hadn't lost Emily's friendship after all. She smiled back at her, knowing that she had made the right decision, not just for herself, but for the integrity of the entire school community. context:The individual expressed a heightened sense of engagement with a narrative, indicating a deliberate effort to enrich the storytelling experience. keywords: exam, cheating, integrity, dilemma, guilt, future, honesty, classmates, anonymous tip tags: morality, relationship, impact, internal struggle

content:Speaker user says: What advice does the author give for those seeking a personal encounter with Christ and how might it happen in unexpected ways?: "So when the Samaritans came to him, they urged him to stay with them, and he stayed two days. And many more became believers.
When the Samaritan woman ran home to tell her friends and neighbors about this most unusual prophet she had just met at Jacob’s well, she could hardly contain herself. Who could blame her? Here was a Jewish man breaking the rules and customs of that time by engaging in conversation with a woman — and that woman was considered an outcast by Hebrew society. To her further astonishment, this stranger proceeded to tell her all about her life and secret sins. Then, to top that, he even called himself the Messiah!
Well, it was too much to take. She ran away in disbelief, astonished by the confrontation, unable to hold in what had occurred. "Come see," she said, urging others to experience for themselves what she had seen and heard.
How could she have known that daily trek to the well to draw water would lead her to a face-to-face encounter with Jesus? How could she have known that a thirsty pilgrim who asked for a drink that day would dramatically change her life?
When her friends arrived at the well, when they heard this prophet’s convincing words, they declared to her: "We no longer believe just because of what you said. Now we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man really is the Savior of the world."
This beautiful, timeless story dramatically shows what can happen when you experience Jesus. The Samaritan woman found out firsthand who Jesus was, and the same opportunity is available to you!
Tragically, today some people have become secondhand believers in our religion and faith. Some merely subsist on the experiences of grandparents, parents, and others who have gone before them. They never actually encounter the risen Christ themselves.
The great author E. Stanley Jones puts this concept into unforgettable language.
He writes, "This generation is living on leftovers from a previous generation, and most of it is thin, precarious, and inadequate. It is secondhand religion."
Essentially, secondhand religion is nothing more than hand-me-down faith that will prove woefully insufficient in the topsy-turvy world. The fact that anything can happen to us at any moment gives us proof that we need a personal Savior, someone we know firsthand, who is present all the time and in every place.
Now I know there are people who do not believe they are capable of having this encounter with Christ. Such talk of having a religious experience leaves them questioning the sanity of those who have. If you are a person who is looking for something to happen that will assure you of God’s presence, then you probably will not find it. That is because you are failing to understand that the presence of God and the availability of Christ already is woven into the fabric of your ordinary life!
Was there a time when you received uncommon strength that sustained you through troubled times? God was in that! Have you ever experienced the joy that comes in rendering help to someone who had no way of returning the favor? God was in that, too!
Take the time to earnestly seek the Mind that has plans for you, the Heart that loves you, and the Hand that moves in your everyday affairs. Then you will be closer than ever to having that religious experience!
That encounter with Christ is waiting to happen, and it may come at the most unexpected time. He could reveal Himself to you in the silence of a hospital waiting room, in the golden beauty of a sunrise or sunset, in a teen’s smile at a school event, in the midst of worship or prayer.
If you are open to the revelation that God has in store for you, it will happen!
Perhaps you have seen the movie "Ben Hur" or read the book. The writer of the novel, from which the movie was made in 1959, was Lew Wallace. Wallace was born in 1827 and was the son of an Indiana governor. After the Civil War, he returned to his law practice in Indianapolis. He then drifted West and settled in New Mexico, where he served as territorial governor (1878-1881).
While he was governor, Wallace was challenged by agnostic Robert Ingersoll to write a book on the life of Jesus. Ingersoll said Jesus should be pictured as a good man — and only a man.
At the time, Wallace himself was not a Christian, but he accepted Ingersoll’s challenge and set about writing a fictional account of the conversion of Judah Ben-Hur. In researching the Gospels for his novel, Wallace opened himself to the life-saving Good News of the Bible and met Jesus Christ face-to-face. He not only became a Christian, but also was born again into the awareness that Jesus is indeed the Savior of the world.

content:Speaker assistant says: The principles of humanitarian aid can be applied to assist displaced persons affected by natural disasters in the following ways:

1. Humanity: The affected persons should be treated with compassion and empathy. Humanitarian assistance should be provided to alleviate their suffering caused by the disaster.

2. Neutrality: Humanitarian assistance should be provided without any prejudice or favoritism. All affected persons should receive aid irrespective of their religion, race or nationality.

3. Impartiality: All affected persons should receive aid according to their needs, and not based on any other factor such as economic or political influence.

4. Independence: Humanitarian aid should be provided independently of any other agenda or interest. It should not be used for any other purpose except for helping the affected persons. 

5. Sustainability: Aid should be provided in a sustainable manner. It should not create dependencies but should promote self-sufficiency, resilience and long-term development.

6. Participation: The affected persons should be involved in the process of aid delivery. They should be consulted and their opinions, needs and priorities should be taken into account to ensure that the assistance provided is relevant and appropriate.

By applying these principles, humanitarian actors can help to ensure that displaced persons affected by natural disasters receive the assistance they require to recover from the disaster and rebuild their lives. context:crisis response keywords: humanitarian aid, displaced persons, disaster relief, empathy, neutrality, sustainability tags: empathy
